rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical separations while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test a substantial temperature increase while keeping the gradient unchanged to probe selectivity in the central cluster and late coeluting pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room to slow the gradient later if needed.

Reduce the gradient slope at the better-performing temperature to test whether the three critical pairs separate as their elution compositions shift. The short elution window in injection 2 provides substantial room to improve resolution without a time penalty.

Keep the shallower gradient that resolved the central cluster and lower temperature to shift the remaining close pair. This tests temperature selectivity while retaining some margin below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Continue the temperature comparison at the shallow slope: moving below 50 C may separate the central pair on the opposite side of its coelution point. This also tests whether the later close pair separates after an elution-order reversal, with the last peak expected near 10 minutes.

At 60 C, the shallow gradient resolved every pair except one apparent crossover. Extending the gradient to 28 minutes tests separation beyond that crossover while placing the last peak approximately at the 10-minute threshold.

Test the steeper-slope side of the late-pair crossover seen near 24 minutes, aiming to separate that pair without a time penalty. An 18-minute gradient may retain enough of the central-cluster resolution gained between the 10- and 24-minute gradients.

Use a slope equivalent to an 18.9-minute gradient over the original composition range, targeting the narrow balance between central-cluster improvement and late-pair deterioration. The 0.55 endpoint remains above the predicted elution composition of the last peak.

Injection 8 reached the maximum CRF; now test a higher starting organic fraction at the same slope to shorten elution while preserving full resolution. Retain injection 8 as the benchmark because its critical pairs have little resolution margin.

Slightly flatten the gradient at the higher starting composition to recover central-cluster resolution while retaining some of the time savings. The later critical pairs in injection 9 provide limited room for this adjustment; injection 8 remains the fully resolved benchmark.

The higher-starting-composition trials trade one critical separation against another, so test a lower-temperature selectivity regime with a shorter gradient. This may resolve the central cluster on the opposite side of its temperature-dependent crossovers while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Lower temperature one grid step while retaining the gradient from injection 11 to test whether both remaining central separations improve. The late peaks have resolution margin, and the last peak should remain near the penalty-free window; injection 8 remains the best method.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction permits a steeper gradient without losing central-cluster resolution. This explores the other side of the starting-composition tradeoff while retaining injection 8 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 8 to locate the shortest fully resolved method near the successful operating point. The central pairs are expected to approach R = 1.5, while the later critical pair should gain separation; retain injection 8 if either central pair falls below threshold.

Test a one-step temperature decrease at the faster, higher-starting-composition method to measure whether selectivity can recover its deficient central pair. Injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this trial explores a potentially faster operating region rather than further steepening its already marginal gradient.

Test a higher starting fraction with a slightly shallower slope in the promising low-temperature regime from injection 11. This may improve the central separations while advancing the late peaks; injection 8 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether ending the gradient near the central cluster’s elution composition lets the subsequent hold recover resolution after a faster initial ramp. The lower endpoint may delay the last peak, so this is a targeted endpoint-selectivity experiment; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Combine a higher starting fraction to advance elution with a shallower gradient to improve the low-temperature central cluster. This tests an alternative route to full resolution near the benchmark’s elution time, while preserving injection 8 as the best method.

Flatten the gradient at the promising conditions from injection 18 to seek full resolution of both central pairs. The last peak has sufficient margin below 10 minutes, and injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test whether lower temperature separates the central crossover seen in injection 19, while a higher starting fraction offsets the longer retention. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved alternative; injection 8 remains the established maximum-score method.

Extend the gradient to improve the sole unresolved pair from injection 20, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes. If full resolution is achieved, a higher starting fraction can then be tested for time savings; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature method from injection 21. Keeping the gradient duration unchanged also slightly reduces its slope, which may help preserve the critical central separation.

Test whether another increase in starting organic fraction separates the central pair beyond the apparent crossover in injection 22 while further shortening elution. All other pairs there had substantial resolution margin; injection 8 remains the fastest established maximum-score method.

Raise the starting fraction one more grid step to shorten the newly fully resolved method. Injection 23 provides a faster maximum-score fallback if compression of the early or central peaks pushes any pair below R = 1.5.

Back off to the fully resolved starting composition from injection 23 and shorten the gradient to seek faster elution without the central-pair compression caused by phi0 = 0.40. Retain injection 23 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method if this final trial loses baseline resolution.
